claims.text: Acid-etching dealloying of the automotive HEA catalyst will form a Pt-rich or noble-metal-enriched surface shell.
A Pt-rich protective shell will minimize surface degradation and poisoning.
The intervention will mitigate activity loss and durability limitations under transient, low-temperature exhaust conditions.
The intervention will retain low overall platinum-group-metal consumption.
The starting catalyst is a homogeneous, nearly equiatomic high-entropy solid solution containing platinum-group and other transition metals.
Acid etching will selectively leach less noble elements from the catalyst surface.
Selective surface leaching will leave a controlled Pt-rich shell over a high-entropy core.
The treated catalyst will have a core-shell structure with a high-entropy-alloy interior and a noble-metal-enriched exterior.
The treated surface will exhibit enhanced metal-nitrogen bonding.
Preferential removal of less noble elements will alter the surface electronic structure.
The altered surface electronic structure will improve adsorption and desorption dynamics of key reactants.
The surface modification will strengthen the fidelity of active sites.
The Pt-rich shell will suppress metal dissolution.
The Pt-rich shell will resist poisoning by H2O and NO.
Suppressed dissolution and poisoning will improve durability under cyclic thermal and chemical stresses.
The acid-etched catalyst will maintain higher activity and degrade more slowly than the untreated HEA catalyst.
The treated catalyst will use a lower total amount of platinum-group metals than the untreated catalyst.
The untreated catalyst is prone to activity loss from surface oxidation, poisoning, and structural degradation during transient exhaust operation.
The intervention is expected to be effective at approximately 100–300 degrees Celsius under moderate H2O and NO exposure.

contradictions.description: The mediator and mechanism invoke enhanced M–N bonding, but the proposed acid-etching and optional annealing intervention introduces no nitrogen source. The cited M–N mechanism pertains to an explicitly N-doped catalyst.

The intervention specifies selective removal of less noble elements and retention or enrichment of Pt at the surface, whereas the predicted outcome claims a lower total PGM amount than in the untreated catalyst. No PGM-loading reduction step is specified.
